headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared file/MCP workflows; compliance mismatch is also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads and writes filesystem content and exposes stdin/stdout and API surfaces; Agent B uses MCP and broad networked plugins. That creates a plausible default pathway where A-generated or user-supplied files are consumed by B as instructions, especially through shared workspace or plugin inputs. The pair lacks provenance controls in the profiles, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests files or tool outputs produced by Agent A without provenance filtering, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a workspace or memory store, attacker-controlled content can bridge them.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of Agent A outputs into Agent B.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
Require manual review before B executes instructions from A.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization and allowlist parsing in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches configuration secrets and can read/write local files; Agent B has broad network egress and plugin/API access. If they share a workspace or memory store, sensitive A-side data can flow into B and then out to third-party services. The profiles do not show isolation or redaction by default, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF Agent A stores secrets or papers in a shared directory, Agent B can read them.
IF Agent B forwards its context to external model providers or plugins, leaked data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Disable B access to A's working directory.
Redact secrets before any handoff.
requires-engineering: add per-field data-loss-prevention filters at the orchestrator boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; Agent B can also write the filesystem and coordinate via shared memory store. Even though A cannot modify git state, overlapping writes to shared files or application state can still race in default multi-instance setups. The conflict is real but narrower than full unrestricted shared-dir mutation.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or memory-backed artifact, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF the orchestrator does not lock shared resources, concurrent updates can corrupt state.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Turn off concurrent runs for shared artifacts.
Snapshot state before each agent run.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing/RAG system that can emit answers and citations, while Agent B is an orchestration layer that can call plugins and act on application context. If B treats A's output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations from A can cascade into downstream actions. Because no verification step is documented, the interaction is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF Agent B uses Agent A's text as a source of truth, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF B triggers plugins or external APIs based on A's output, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require citation checks before reuse.
Add a human approval step for actions.
Compare A outputs against source documents.
Limit B to read-only summarization of A.
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating and verification policies.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles academic papers plus configuration secrets, while Agent B handles application context and sends data to Azure/OpenAI-style providers and MCP/OpenAPI tools. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or DPA alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible. Because the data classes differ and B is externally networked, the conservative severity is medium.
conditions: IF EU personal data or regulated content is routed through B's external providers, residency or DPA obligations may be triggered.
IF A's secrets are logged or retained by B's plugins, retention policy mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Classify data before handoff.
Block regulated data from external APIs.
Review provider DPAs and residency settings.
Shorten log retention.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
